analysis.one_liner: Makes online marketplaces liable for counterfeit health-and-safety goods unless they verify and screen sellers.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee in May 2021 and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would change trademark law so that an online shopping platform can be held legally responsible when a third-party seller uses a counterfeit mark on goods that implicate health and safety — things like medicine, car parts, or children's products. A platform could escape that liability only by taking specified steps before an infringement happens: verifying each seller's identity and US contact for lawsuits, requiring sellers to promise not to sell fakes, using technology to screen listings for counterfeits before they go public, removing suspicious listings, and banning repeat offenders. It applies to platforms with at least $500,000 in annual sales, and to smaller ones after they get ten warning notices. The bill never left the Senate Judiciary Committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Shoppers who could be harmed by counterfeit versions of health-and-safety goods, and brand-name companies whose trademarks are copied. Consumers get a safer supply of goods sold online; trademark holders get platforms screening for fakes at no cost to the brand.

how_it_helps.text: The bill makes an e-commerce platform contributoryily liable for a third-party seller's use of a counterfeit mark on goods that implicate health and safety, unless the platform took specified preventive steps before the infringement.

To avoid liability, a platform must verify each seller's identity and principal place of business with reliable documentation, require a US registered agent or verified address for service of process, and obtain a seller attestation that goods bearing registered marks are authentic.

Platforms must run proactive technology to screen listings for counterfeit marks before display, remove listings when reasonably aware of counterfeits, terminate sellers with repeated counterfeit use (three listings in one year counts), and block terminated sellers from rejoining under new aliases — all at no cost to the trademark registrant.

Platforms must display each seller's verified business information and the country the goods ship from and were manufactured in, and listings must use images that accurately depict the actual goods for sale.
The liability rule covers any platform with annual sales of at least $500,000, and reaches smaller platforms after they receive ten aggregate notices identifying potentially counterfeit listings.

analysis.who_pays: Large online marketplaces bear the compliance cost — seller verification, screening technology, and takedown programs — and face lawsuits if they fall short. Some costs would likely reach consumers as higher fees, and the verification requirements could squeeze small or overseas sellers off the platforms entirely.
analysis.who_pays_short: Large online marketplaces and small third-party sellers

drawbacks.text: The compliance burden is heavy: platforms must verify seller identities, provide US points of contact for lawsuits, and run screening and takedown technology at no cost to the trademark owner, which could raise selling fees and consumer prices on major marketplaces.

Requiring a US registered agent or verified US address for service of process could push small sellers — including overseas-based ones — off major platforms, shrinking the selection and low prices those marketplaces offer.

The definition of 'goods that implicate health and safety' is broad, covering goods whose use 'can lead to illness, disease, injury... or death' if not compliant with regulations and industry standards, so the liability rule could sweep in many ordinary product categories and invite costly disputes over removal decisions.

Fear of liability could lead platforms to over-remove legitimate listings, since the bill lets platforms disable listings based on general circumstances amounting to 'reasonable awareness' of counterfeit use.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The consumer-safety goal is real: counterfeits of medicines, auto parts, and children's products genuinely injure people, and platform-level screening is the practical way to catch them at scale. But the bill shifts nearly all the enforcement cost onto platforms and their users rather than the trademark owners who benefit, and its broad definitions and verification requirements risk raising prices and pushing small sellers off the internet's largest marketplaces. A narrower, better-cost-balanced version could plausibly achieve most of the safety gain.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee, where it sat without a hearing, markup, or floor vote until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Christopher Coons introduced the bill on May 26, 2021, joined by Sen. Thom Tillis, and it was read twice and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee the same day.
No further action was taken: the action history shows only the introduction and the referral, and the bill died in committee when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large online marketplaces, which avoided new liability and compliance costs, along with sellers of counterfeit goods, who faced no new screening requirement. Consumers got no added protection against counterfeit health-and-safety products.

for.name: Sen. Christopher Coons
for.what_they_did: Introduced the SHOP SAFE Act and championed platform liability for counterfeit health-and-safety goods.

for.name: Sen. Thom Tillis
for.role: Original cosponsor; member, Senate Judiciary Committee
for.what_they_did: Signed on as the bill's sole cosponsor at introduction, giving it bipartisan sponsorship in the Judiciary Committee's jurisdiction.

against.name: Senate Judiciary Committee
against.role: Committee of referral (Chair: Sen. Richard Durbin, D-IL)
against.what_they_did: Received the referred bill and took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: Both sponsors were Senate Judiciary members from opposite parties — Sen. Coons, a Democrat, and Sen. Tillis, the bill's only cosponsor and one of the Senate's 50 Republicans — and no recorded opposition ever appeared, but the committee never acted on it either way.

industries.note: The bill would impose liability plus mandatory seller-verification, screening, and takedown programs on any platform with $500,000+ in annual sales, at the platform's own expense. Its failure leaves marketplaces free of this liability, while shoppers remain exposed to counterfeit health-and-safety goods.

Registrants would get platform screening, seller verification, and takedown programs at no cost to them, cutting into counterfeit sales. Here the brands' interest in stopping fakes runs alongside consumers' interest in safer products, though the public picks up the enforcement cost through platform fees and prices.

industries.industry: Third-party sellers, especially small and overseas-based sellers
industries.note: Legitimate sellers would benefit from less competition with counterfeiters, but the requirement to maintain a US registered agent or verified US address could push small and overseas sellers off major platforms entirely.
The bill targets counterfeiters directly, requiring platforms to prescreen listings, remove suspect ones, and permanently ban repeat offenders. What it costs them is what shoppers would gain.
